justice: Most of the visible street space is allocated to multiple wide motor-vehicle lanes, while no clear sidewalk or dedicated pedestrian zone is visible along the roadway.
A zebra crossing is painted across the carriageway, but there are no visible refuge islands, pedestrian signals, or curb ramps to support equal use by all road users.
The right side is bordered by a guardrail and water edge, and the left side appears to have only a narrow roadside margin, limiting accessible space for non-drivers.
safety: The road is very wide and open, which can encourage higher vehicle speeds and increases exposure for anyone using the painted crosswalk.
The visible crossing is only paint on the pavement; there is no raised median, traffic light, or other physical protection to reduce pedestrian-vehicle conflict.
A guardrail separates the road from the waterside edge, which helps prevent run-off crashes, but it does not improve crossing safety for people on foot.
livability: The setting is dominated by asphalt, traffic lanes, utility poles, and open water, with very few visible destinations or active street-front uses that support daily street life.
There are no visible benches, bus stops, shopfronts, or gathering spaces that would make the corridor socially active or supportive of everyday public life.
The surrounding environment appears sparse and infrastructure-oriented, so the street functions mainly as a through-road rather than a place for community activity.
sustainability: There is no visible dedicated bike lane, transit stop, or other clear support for low-carbon travel modes besides the basic road corridor.
Vegetation is limited to narrow roadside planting and low greenery, with little tree canopy or shade-producing green infrastructure visible.
The adjacent water body adds environmental openness, but there are no visible permeable plazas, bioswales, or other stormwater features integrated into the street edge.
aesthetics: The broad view over the water and the open sky creates a visually expansive landscape with some scenic value.
The roadway surface and lane markings appear orderly and well maintained, which gives the corridor a clean and coherent appearance.
However, the scene is visually dominated by wide asphalt pavement, utility lines, poles, and sparse roadside treatment, reducing richness and human-scale character.
comfort: There is almost no visible shade from street trees or shelters, so thermal comfort would be poor in hot or sunny weather.
No benches, resting areas, or protected pedestrian spaces are visible, limiting physical comfort for people outside vehicles.
The wide exposed roadway and presence of trucks and cars suggest a noisy, psychologically uncomfortable environment for non-motorized users.
walkability: A painted zebra crossing is present, but there is no visible continuous sidewalk network connecting to it on either side of the road.
The crossing spans a very wide carriageway without a median refuge, making walking routes feel long and exposed.
The corridor lacks pedestrian-scale elements such as shade trees, seating, active frontages, and clear separation from fast traffic, all of which weaken walking appeal.
